newsitem.title: USA: Swiss appeal for fairness on Nazi gold issue.
newsitem.headline: Swiss appeal for fairness on Nazi gold issue.

text.p: Swiss parliamentarians responding to bad publicity about their country appealed on Wednesday for patience and fairness as they try to make amends for the Swiss handling of Nazi gold a half-century ago.

The legislators, in Washington to meet administration and congressional officials, said the Swiss were obligated to take action after a new U.S. report on Nazi-Swiss gold deals, but needed time to gather facts and rethink their history.

One legislator said it was "incredible" that a New York Times editorial on Wednesday suggested the United States could freeze some Swiss assets if Switzerland did not change the postwar balance sheet that left it holding much of the gold the Nazis took from other countries and Holocaust victims.

"Do you think that is a fair discussion between people?" Swiss Senator Gian-Reto Plattner asked reporters, referring to the editorial. The part suggesting the United States could freeze some Swiss assets is "an incredible paragraph," he said.
Switzerland needs to re-evaluate its history, and is undergoing a "necessary crisis" as it looks at its behaviour during and after the Second World War, Plattner said.

"Switzerland recognises its moral obligation to do much more than has been done in the last 50 years, when essentially nothing at all has been done, and to do more than is now legally binding," Plattner said.

"But if one asks us to be fair, to accept the fact that we have a moral obligation, we ask to be treated fairly. Fair treatment in this context means that it is not we that are singled out as the sole villains, and that it is recognised what we do and what we have done," Plattner said.
Plattner is the president of the Foundation for Humanity and Justice, a private Swiss foundation created recently to provide financial aid to survivors of the Nazi Holocaust.

Plattner and Lili Nabbolz, a member of the Swiss House of Representatives, met this week with Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat and historian Wiliam Slany, authors of the U.S. report on Nazi gold deals with Switzerland and other countries.

The report, released last week, said Switzerland handed over to the Allies just $58 million worth of Nazi gold after the war, although there may have been more than $400 million in German-looted gold in Switzerland at the time.
The report also said some gold the Nazis sold to the Swiss was taken from Holocaust victims, even from their teeth.
Plattner and Nabbolz, who met with reporters at the Swiss embassy, said they welcomed the U.S. report but it was far from the end of the fact-gathering process.

They said Switzerland favoured an international conference on the Nazi era to convene later this year. Switzerland has a historical commission in Switzerland investigating the Swiss role as a financial centre during the war, and a banking commission with the mandate to search for unclaimed accounts of Holocaust survivors.

The Swiss government set up a Holocaust memorial fund with $182 million in donations from banks and businesses. The Swiss president also proposed a $4.7 billion "Solidarity Foundation" that would finance aid to victims of disasters and human rights outrages, including the Holocaust, but made it subject to voter approval in a referendum.

Plattner and Nabbolz said the referendum would not take place before next year. Some people in the country had not yet absorbed the Eizenstat report, they said, partly because for so long there had been a focus on the "shiny" side, not the "dark" side of Swiss wartime neutrality.

"People felt somehow accused ... to defend what they had not caused," Nabbolz said. Some people questioned why Switzerland is being criticised when it was the Germans who looted the gold, Plattner said.

The government will have to educate people about the need for the foundation, Nabbolz said, because it could not make people "spend billions for something they do not understand. You cannot make them understand with a hammer in your hand."
Plattner added, "Please be a little patient, don't run us into a corner." Then, "Swiss-American relations would be at a freezing point, and who the hell wants this?"
